nameStory: Creeping spearwort gets its name from two distinctive behaviors: it 'creeps' along the ground by sending out runners like a strawberry plant, and its leaves are shaped like narrow spear points. The word 'spearwort' is an old English term meaning 'spear-shaped plant,' perfectly describing those slender, pointed leaves that distinguish it from its rounder-leaved buttercup cousins.
description: Creeping spearwort is a small, low-growing member of the buttercup family that hugs wet ground with its creeping stems. Unlike the familiar buttercups with their deeply divided leaves, this little plant has simple, narrow leaves that look almost grass-like. It produces tiny yellow flowers typical of buttercups but stays close to the ground, rarely reaching more than a few inches tall. Think of it as a miniature buttercup that decided to become a ground-hugger.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, spear-shaped leaves that feel smooth and somewhat fleshy, completely unlike the deeply divided leaves of most buttercups - they look almost grass-like but are attached individually to the stem

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Creeps along the ground with trailing runners that root at nodes, forming small colonies in wet spots - you can often trace the connecting stems between individual plants

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny yellow flowers with 5 petals that have the classic buttercup shine, but much smaller than common buttercups - about the size of your pinky nail

idTips.label: Habitat Clue
idTips.description: Always found in wet, muddy areas where the soil stays moist - if your shoes are getting wet, you're in the right habitat for this plant

habitat: Creeping spearwort thrives in wet, muddy areas throughout New England, particularly along pond edges, in marshes, and in wet meadows where the soil stays consistently moist. Look for it in places where water levels fluctuate seasonally, such as the muddy margins of ponds and slow streams. It prefers full sun to partial shade and can tolerate temporary flooding.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges early as small rosettes of narrow leaves, with runners beginning to extend from established plants. The creeping habit becomes most obvious as winter-killed stems are replaced by fresh growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with tiny yellow flowers appearing from June through August. The creeping runners are actively growing and rooting, making this the best time to observe the characteristic spreading habit.
seasonality.fall: Flowering may continue into early fall in favorable conditions. Seeds ripen and disperse, while the creeping stems continue to establish new root systems at nodes.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground portions die back in freezing weather, but established root systems survive to regrow in spring. Look for dried, matted stems marking where colonies grew the previous year.

funFact: Despite being in the buttercup family, creeping spearwort has figured out how to live an almost amphibious lifestyle - it can actually survive being completely underwater for weeks during spring floods, then continue growing normally when the water recedes, making it one of nature's most adaptable buttercups.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with young grass shoots due to its narrow leaves, but remember the key difference: grass leaves emerge from a sheath and have parallel veins, while spearwort leaves are attached individually to the stem with a network of veins. If you see tiny yellow buttercup flowers, you've definitely found spearwort, not grass!
contextualKnowledge: The name 'spearwort' might sound intimidating, but don't worry - it's completely unrelated to any dangerous plants and simply refers to the spear-shaped leaves. However, like all buttercups, it does contain mild toxins that make it unpalatable to most animals, which is why you'll often see it thriving in areas where cattle or deer graze heavily.
compareHints: Among New England's buttercups, creeping spearwort is unique for its simple, narrow leaves - all other local buttercups have divided or lobed leaves. Its closest relative is lesser spearwort, which is taller and doesn't creep along the ground with runners. While creeping buttercup also spreads by runners, it has the typical three-part divided buttercup leaves rather than the simple spear-shaped ones.

Among New England's many buttercup species, bulbous buttercup is the only one with that distinctive swollen stem base.
